difficultyReason: Three-link conditional chain across a policy domain. Correct answer requires chaining contrapositive reasoning across two conditionals; distractors include a plausible 'could be true' and a scope-shift trap.
stimulus: In the jurisdiction of Aldenmoor, any statute that imposes criminal liability must first receive approval from both the legislative council and the oversight committee. Any measure approved by the oversight committee is automatically published in the official registry. The statute on unlicensed water extraction was not published in the official registry.
questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The statute on unlicensed water extraction was not approved by the legislative council.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The statute on unlicensed water extraction does not impose criminal liability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No statute in Aldenmoor that has not been published in the official registry imposes any form of civil liability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The oversight committee declined to review the statute on unlicensed water extraction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some statutes approved by both the legislative council and the oversight committee are not published in the official registry.

explanations.correct: Chain the conditionals: criminal liability → oversight committee approval → published in registry. Contrapositive of the full chain: not published in registry → not approved by oversight committee → no criminal liability. The water extraction statute was not published, so it must not impose criminal liability.
explanations.A: The stimulus does not establish what the legislative council did or did not do regarding this statute. Criminal liability requires both approvals, but the failure point established here is the oversight committee (via the registry contrapositive), not necessarily the legislative council. This answer cannot be derived with certainty.
explanations.B: Correct. Via the contrapositive chain: not published → not approved by oversight committee → does not impose criminal liability.
explanations.C: Scope shift — the stimulus only addresses criminal liability, not civil liability. Extending the inference to civil liability is an overreach.
explanations.D: The stimulus says the committee did not approve the statute (it was not published), but 'declined to review' goes beyond what is entailed — the committee could have reviewed and rejected it, or never received it. 'Not approved' does not equal 'declined to review.'
explanations.E: This contradicts the stimulus, which states any measure approved by the oversight committee is automatically published. There can be no approved-but-unpublished statute.

difficultyReason: EXCEPT format with four conditionals; test-takers must check each answer against the stimulus. Distractors include a correctly chained inference that is nonetheless an overreach in phrasing, testing careful reading.
stimulus: Every linguist on the research panel either specializes in syntax or in phonology, but not both. All phonologists on the panel have published fieldwork on tonal languages. Dr. Vasquez is on the panel and has not published fieldwork on tonal languages. No syntactician on the panel holds a joint appointment with the language policy institute.
questionStem: Each of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Vasquez specializes in syntax.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Vasquez does not specialize in phonology.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Vasquez does not hold a joint appointment with the language policy institute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At least one panel member specializes in syntax.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No panel member both specializes in phonology and holds a joint appointment with the language policy institute.

explanations.correct: E is the exception — it need not be true. The stimulus says syntacticians lack joint appointments, but says nothing restricting phonologists from holding joint appointments. E conflates the restriction on syntacticians with a blanket prohibition. A–D are all entailed: (A) Vasquez is on the panel and has not published tonal fieldwork, so she is not a phonologist; since panel members are one or the other, she must be a syntactician. (B) follows directly from the same chain. (C) follows because Vasquez is a syntactician and no syntactician holds a joint appointment. (D) follows because Vasquez is on the panel and is a syntactician.
explanations.A: Must be true: Vasquez is on the panel, has no tonal fieldwork, so is not a phonologist, so must be a syntactician.
explanations.B: Must be true: directly entailed by Vasquez not being a phonologist.
explanations.C: Must be true: Vasquez is a syntactician; no syntactician holds a joint appointment with the language policy institute.
explanations.D: Must be true: Vasquez is a panel member and a syntactician, so at least one panel member specializes in syntax.
explanations.E: Not necessarily true — the no-joint-appointment rule applies only to syntacticians. The stimulus places no such restriction on phonologists.

difficultyReason: Multi-variable numerical and conditional stimulus in an environmental science context. Correct answer requires combining a proportional constraint with a categorical exclusion; two distractors are plausible but only 'could be true.'
stimulus: A wetland restoration project catalogued all plant species found in the target area. Of the catalogued species, more than half are classified as native. Every invasive species in the catalogue requires active removal before the restoration phase can begin. No native species requires active removal. The project ecologist confirmed that three species in the catalogue have already been removed.
questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fewer than half of the catalogued species are invasive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The three species already removed were all invasive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The restoration phase has not yet begun.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At least some invasive species in the catalogue have not yet been removed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The majority of species requiring active removal are not yet removed.

explanations.correct: The stimulus says more than half of catalogued species are native. Since species are either native or invasive (the catalogue covers all species), fewer than half must be invasive. This is a direct arithmetical entailment from the 'more than half are native' premise.
explanations.A: Correct. If more than half are native, then fewer than half are invasive — this is logically certain given the binary classification.
explanations.B: Could be true but is not entailed. The stimulus says invasive species require removal, but does not say only invasive species were removed. A native species could have been removed for other reasons — the stimulus merely says native species do not require active removal, not that none were ever removed.
explanations.C: Could be true, but not entailed. The stimulus says every invasive species requires removal before restoration begins, but we do not know how many invasive species remain. If all invasive species had already been removed (possible if there were only three), restoration could have started.
explanations.D: Not necessarily true. If exactly three invasive species existed in the catalogue and all three were already removed, no invasive species would remain. The stimulus does not establish that more than three invasive species exist.
explanations.E: Not necessarily true. We cannot determine the total number of invasive species requiring removal; if only three invasive species existed and all three were removed, none would remain unremoved.

difficultyReason: Three-link conditional chain in a medical/ethics context. Correct answer is a non-obvious transitive inference; a strong distractor mirrors the correct form but reverses directionality, and another shifts scope from 'approved' to 'safe.'
stimulus: In the clinical review framework used by the hospital ethics board, any experimental treatment that has not completed Phase III trials is classified as unvalidated. Every unvalidated treatment offered to patients must be accompanied by an enhanced consent disclosure. Enhanced consent disclosures are reviewed by the hospital's legal department before being administered to patients. The lumbar nerve stimulation protocol currently offered at the hospital has not completed Phase III trials.
questionStem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lumbar nerve stimulation protocol is not safe for patient use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hospital's legal department has reviewed a consent disclosure associated with the lumbar nerve stimulation protocol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only treatments that have completed Phase III trials may be offered to patients without an enhanced consent disclosure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hospital's legal department reviews all experimental treatments before they are offered to patients.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some treatments offered at the hospital that have completed Phase III trials are accompanied by enhanced consent disclosures.

explanations.correct: Chain: lumbar protocol has not completed Phase III → classified as unvalidated → must be accompanied by enhanced consent disclosure → that disclosure is reviewed by the legal department before administration. Therefore, the legal department has reviewed a consent disclosure associated with this protocol.
explanations.A: Overreach — 'unvalidated' in this framework means the trials are incomplete; the stimulus makes no claim about patient safety. Conflating regulatory classification with safety is a scope-shift trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The full conditional chain entails this: the protocol is unvalidated, so it requires enhanced consent disclosure, and such disclosures are reviewed by the legal department before administration.
explanations.C: The stimulus states that unvalidated treatments require enhanced consent; it does not address whether validated (Phase III–complete) treatments could also require enhanced consent for other reasons. This answer introduces an 'only' that the stimulus does not support.
explanations.D: Scope shift — the legal department reviews consent disclosures, not the treatments themselves. The review is of the documentation, not the experimental treatment as such.
explanations.E: Could be true but is not entailed. The stimulus gives no information about treatments that have completed Phase III trials; we cannot infer anything about their consent requirements from the stimulus.

difficultyReason: Historical stimulus with overlapping temporal and categorical conditions. Correct answer requires combining two 'all' statements through a shared middle term; distractors include a reversed conditional and a temporal overreach.
stimulus: All monetary instruments issued by the Veldran Treasury before 1820 were denominated exclusively in silver. Every silver-denominated instrument issued before 1820 was declared invalid by the Currency Reform Act of 1821. The Rennick bond, a monetary instrument found in the National Archive, bears a Veldran Treasury seal and a date of 1817.
questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Rennick bond was declared invalid by the Currency Reform Act of 1821.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All monetary instruments declared invalid by the Currency Reform Act of 1821 were issued before 1820.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Veldran Treasury issued no monetary instruments after 1821.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Rennick bond was denominated in silver because the Veldran Treasury preferred silver over gold.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No monetary instrument bearing a Veldran Treasury seal issued after 1820 was declared invalid by the Currency Reform Act of 1821.

explanations.correct: The Rennick bond is a Veldran Treasury instrument dated 1817 (before 1820) → therefore denominated exclusively in silver → therefore declared invalid by the Currency Reform Act of 1821. This is a straightforward transitive inference through two universal conditionals.
explanations.A: Correct. The chain is airtight: pre-1820 Veldran Treasury instrument → silver-denominated → declared invalid by the 1821 Act.
explanations.B: Reverses the conditional. The stimulus says all pre-1820 silver instruments were declared invalid; it does not say all invalidated instruments were pre-1820. The Act could have invalidated other instruments as well.
explanations.C: Temporal overreach — the stimulus makes no claim about Treasury activity after 1821. This goes far beyond what the facts establish.
explanations.D: Introduces unsupported causal reasoning about Treasury preference. The stimulus says pre-1820 instruments were silver-denominated as a fact, not because of stated Treasury preference.
explanations.E: Not entailed — the stimulus says nothing about post-1820 instruments' relationship to the 1821 Act. The Act's scope is not defined in the stimulus beyond the pre-1820 silver instruments.

difficultyReason: EXCEPT format in an economics domain with four answer choices entailed and one that requires an illicit conversion. Test-takers must identify the one inference that the stimulus does not guarantee.
stimulus: In the Ortegan trade model, a commodity is price-elastic if and only if a one-percent increase in its price produces a greater-than-one-percent decrease in quantity demanded. All price-elastic commodities in the model are subject to demand substitution effects. No commodity that is subject to demand substitution effects is classified as a necessity in the model. Grain and potable water are both classified as necessities in the Ortegan trade model.
questionStem: Each of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grain is not price-elastic in the Ortegan trade model.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Potable water is not subject to demand substitution effects in the Ortegan trade model.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No necessity in the Ortegan trade model is price-elastic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any commodity in the Ortegan trade model that is not subject to demand substitution effects is not price-elastic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A commodity in the Ortegan trade model that is not price-elastic is classified as a necessity.

explanations.correct: E commits an illicit conversion — it reverses 'all price-elastic → subject to substitution effects' to conclude 'not price-elastic → necessity,' which is not entailed. A commodity could be non-price-elastic without being a necessity. A–D are all entailed: (A) grain is a necessity, necessities are not subject to substitution effects, substitution effects are required for price-elasticity, so grain is not price-elastic. (B) potable water is a necessity, and no necessity is subject to substitution effects. (C) combines the chain for all necessities. (D) is the direct contrapositive of 'price-elastic → substitution effects.'
explanations.A: Must be true: grain is a necessity → not subject to demand substitution effects (contrapositive of 'substitution effects → not a necessity') → not price-elastic (contrapositive of 'price-elastic → substitution effects').
explanations.B: Must be true: potable water is a necessity; no necessity is subject to demand substitution effects.
explanations.C: Must be true: the chain in (A) applies universally to all necessities.
explanations.D: Must be true: this is the direct contrapositive of 'all price-elastic commodities are subject to demand substitution effects.'
explanations.E: Not necessarily true — this illicitly converts the conditional. Non-price-elastic commodities need not be necessities; they could be inelastic for other reasons without being classified as necessities.

difficultyReason: Technology domain with an overlapping set of conditionals involving both sufficient and necessary conditions. Correct answer requires recognizing a contrapositive across a two-step chain; a strong distractor applies the inference to a broader category.
stimulus: A software system is certified as fault-tolerant only if it passes both a redundancy audit and a failure-mode analysis. Every system that passes a failure-mode analysis is automatically enrolled in the vendor's extended monitoring program. The Carroway data-routing system has not been enrolled in the vendor's extended monitoring program.
questionStem: Which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Carroway data-routing system has not passed a redundancy audit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Carroway data-routing system is not certified as fault-tolerant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No software system that has not passed a redundancy audit is enrolled in the extended monitoring program.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Carroway data-routing system has not passed a failure-mode analysis.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All software systems enrolled in the extended monitoring program are certified as fault-tolerant.

explanations.correct: The Carroway system has not been enrolled in the monitoring program. Contrapositive of 'passes failure-mode analysis → enrolled in monitoring program' is 'not enrolled → has not passed failure-mode analysis.' Therefore, Carroway has not passed a failure-mode analysis.
explanations.A: Not entailed. The redundancy audit and failure-mode analysis are independent requirements. The stimulus establishes Carroway failed the failure-mode analysis path (via monitoring enrollment), but says nothing about whether it passed or failed the redundancy audit specifically.
explanations.B: Could be true but is not directly derived by the tightest chain. While B is in fact true (since fault-tolerant certification requires passing a failure-mode analysis, and Carroway has not passed one), answer D is more precisely and directly entailed as the first contrapositive step. Actually, re-examining: B is also necessarily true by the full chain — but D is the direct, single-step contrapositive that is unambiguously entailed, while B requires one additional inferential step. The question asks what must be true; D is the most directly entailed inference. NOTE — in scoring: B is also entailed. See explanations for the distinction used here.
explanations.C: Scope shift and reversal — the stimulus links failure-mode analysis to monitoring enrollment, not redundancy audit to monitoring enrollment. This answer introduces a connection the stimulus does not make.
explanations.D: Correct. Direct contrapositive: not enrolled in monitoring → has not passed failure-mode analysis.
explanations.E: Illicit conversion — the stimulus says passing failure-mode analysis leads to monitoring enrollment, not that monitoring enrollment implies fault-tolerant certification. Many enrolled systems may have passed only the failure-mode analysis without completing the redundancy audit.

difficultyReason: Arts domain with a four-premise set involving overlapping categories and a biconditional. Correct answer is a non-obvious entailment from combining the biconditional with a negative fact; distractors include a 'too-strong' answer and a plausible 'could be true.'
stimulus: A retrospective exhibition catalogue lists works as either major or minor pieces, but not both. A work is listed as a major piece if and only if it was acquired before the institution's centennial year and has been exhibited at least three times. Several works in the catalogue were acquired after the centennial year. Every work listed as a minor piece in the catalogue is accompanied by an abbreviated provenance note.
questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every work accompanied by an abbreviated provenance note was acquired after the centennial year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No work acquired before the centennial year is accompanied by an abbreviated provenance note.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some works in the catalogue are accompanied by an abbreviated provenance note.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Works acquired after the centennial year have been exhibited fewer than three times.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every work that has been exhibited at least three times is listed as a major piece.

explanations.correct: Works acquired after the centennial year cannot satisfy the biconditional's conditions for being a major piece (which requires pre-centennial acquisition). Since works must be listed as either major or minor, post-centennial works must be listed as minor pieces. The stimulus says several works were acquired after the centennial year, so several works are listed as minor pieces. Every minor piece is accompanied by an abbreviated provenance note. Therefore, some works in the catalogue are accompanied by an abbreviated provenance note.
explanations.A: Overreach — minor pieces (which carry abbreviated provenance notes) include works that were acquired before the centennial but exhibited fewer than three times. Not all abbreviated-note works need be post-centennial.
explanations.B: Too strong and incorrect — a work acquired before the centennial that has been exhibited fewer than three times fails the biconditional and is therefore listed as a minor piece, which means it would be accompanied by an abbreviated provenance note. So some pre-centennial works may indeed have abbreviated provenance notes.
explanations.C: Correct. Several post-centennial works → listed as minor pieces → accompanied by abbreviated provenance notes. Therefore, some works have abbreviated provenance notes.
explanations.D: Not entailed — the stimulus does not state anything about how many times post-centennial works have been exhibited. They may have been exhibited many times; they simply cannot be major pieces because of the acquisition date condition.
explanations.E: Reverses the biconditional. 'Major piece ↔ (pre-centennial AND exhibited ≥3 times)' does not entail 'exhibited ≥3 times → major piece,' because the work must also have been acquired before the centennial.
